body_markdown:
Colin Chapman would be proud: The team that built the 1993 Porsche 911 Buggy simplified and added lightness. The idea wasn’t to take on the British, however. The one-off buggy was designed to teach students how to drive a 911 the way Porsche intended.


The project started on February 11, 1993, and Porsche assigned the task of turning a 964 into a buggy to a team of apprentices. The goal was to make the coupe light, basic, and, above all, safe so that the instructors at the Porsche Sport Driving School could use it to teach students the fundamentals of driving a 911. The end result is a two-seater that looks ready to star in a *Mad Max* movie.


Most of the body was removed, but the buggy remains instantly recognizable as a 911 thanks to its silhouette and its proportions. In a way, it’s a pure, raw take on the lines that have characterized Porsche’s emblematic sports cars since its inception. There’s a welded roll cage, tubular bumpers on both ends, and custom-made fenders almost reminiscent of what you’d see on a Caterham.

There’s not much left inside, either, beyond a pair of sport seats, five analog gauges, and a three-spoke steering wheel. Every wire, sensor, and cable is visible, which makes the buggy fascinating to look at. It’s almost like seeing a 964 through an X-ray machine.


It doesn’t sound like Porsche made any mechanical modifications to the buggy. It’s based on a 911 Carrera, which used a 3.6-liter air-cooled flat-six rated at 250 horsepower. Porsche chose to link the engine to a four-speed Tiptronic automatic transmission. The engine lid is one of the panels that was removed, so a custom-made, yellow-painted protective cover is bolted over the cooling fan.


Porsche’s apprentices spent 1344 hours building the Speed Yellow-finished buggy over the course of three months. It was unveiled on May 13, 1993, and it joined Porsche’s training program at the Hockenheim Ring in Germany the following year. Participants used it to learn about the 911’s rear-biased handling, notably by taking it for a timed run on a slalom course. Instructors reportedly used the car into the 2000s, which is impressive: This one-of-a-kind buggy survived over a decade’s worth of punishing track use.


When it finally retired, the buggy was sent to Porsche’s massive collection of classics, where it shared warehouse space with one-offs,[prototypes](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/porsche-914-s-prototype-specs-history-pictures/) , and concepts. It returned to the spotlight earlier in 2026 in the most fitting way possible: By participating in the 2026 edition of the[FAT Ice Race](https://www.hagerty.com/media/motorsports/big-sky-low-grip-fat-ice-race-comes-to-montana/) held in Zell am See, Austria. Instead of being taken on a leisurely drive through the countryside, it was fitted with a set of studded snow tires and driven on a frozen lake by Le Mans winners Timo Bernhard and Jörg Bergmeister.


Over three decades after it was built, this buggy is still doing what it was designed to do: Show how entertaining a 911 can be.
